content: This includes providing guidance to state, tribal, territorial, and local Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Programs (CLPPPs) as they expand into broader Healthy Homes initiatives. The goal is to assist these programs and other agencies in developing effective Healthy Homes strategies. Florence Nightingale once emphasized the critical link between health and housing, stating that the connection between the two is one of the most significant relationships that exist. Despite this recognition, much work remains to fully understand and address these connections. In the United States, approximately 38 million homes contain lead-based paint hazards, which can result in childhood lead poisoning. Additionally, around 6 million housing units nationwide are associated with risks such as injuries, respiratory diseases like asthma, and other quality-of-life issues. Homes with moderate or severe physical problems increase the likelihood of fire, electrical injuries, falls, rodent bites, and other health risks. Many of these hazards can be mitigated or eliminated through proper education, home maintenance, and testing. The Healthy People 2020 national health agenda envisions a society where all individuals live long and healthy lives. A Healthy Homes program aligns with this vision by addressing Goal Two: achieving health equity and eliminating health disparities. It also supports eight proposed Environmental Health objectives, including reducing housing units with physical problems, lowering blood lead levels in children, reducing indoor allergen levels, increasing radon mitigation systems in homes, and decreasing the prevalence of lead-based paint hazards. The Surgeon General’s Call to Action to Promote Healthy Homes outlines a coordinated approach to reducing disparities in access to safe, affordable, and environmentally friendly housing. It emphasizes that a healthy home should be designed, built, renovated, and maintained to support the health of its residents. Key features of a healthy home include its construction, design, maintenance, safety devices, indoor air and water quality, chemical presence, resident behavior, and community characteristics. Presidential Executive Order 12898 on Environmental Justice addresses health and housing disparities among minority, low-income, and tribal populations. It underscores the right of all individuals to live in a healthy home and an environment free of hazards. This aligns with the Healthy People 2020 agenda by promoting quality of life and eliminating health and housing inequities. Institutionalizing environmental justice and implementing the Surgeon General’s recommendations are critical steps toward achieving these goals. The CDC’s Healthy Homes Initiative adopts a coordinated, comprehensive, and holistic approach to preventing diseases and injuries caused by housing-related hazards. This initiative aims to expand the scope of single-issue public health programs, such as those focused on childhood lead poisoning or asthma, to address multiple housing deficiencies that impact health and safety. It seeks to build capacity among public health practitioners, nurses, housing specialists, and community workers to develop and manage effective Healthy Homes programs. The initiative also promotes cross-disciplinary activities at various levels—federal, state, tribal, territorial, and community—to address unhealthy and unsafe housing through surveillance, research, and prevention programs. It emphasizes the importance of collecting local data, monitoring progress, conducting research to establish causal links between substandard housing and health outcomes, and developing guidelines to assess and mitigate risks. Additionally, it advocates for low-cost, practical methods to reduce health and safety risks in substandard housing. A comprehensive needs assessment is a critical first step in developing a successful Healthy Homes program. This process involves collecting and analyzing data to understand community demographics, identify health and housing needs, and evaluate program and partner capabilities. The assessment should address community analysis, training and education needs, policy reviews, program experience, partnerships, program evaluation, and surveillance efforts. The findings from the needs assessment should inform the development of a strategic plan, which will serve as a roadmap for addressing identified weaknesses, prioritizing issues, and implementing an effective Healthy Homes program. Community analysis involves understanding the demographics, health issues, and housing needs of the community. Programs should use available data to identify hazards and target specific geographic areas or populations for intervention. Engaging the community through meetings or focus groups can provide additional insights into health and housing needs. Training and education are essential for building a sustainable Healthy Homes program. Training opportunities include courses for health and housing professionals, designers, architects, contractors, nurses, and community health workers. These courses cover topics such as building science, home assessments, and community education on Healthy Homes principles. The CDC Healthy Homes/Lead Poisoning Prevention Training Center offers specialized training tracks in program management, data management, case management, and primary prevention. Policy review is another important component. Programs should identify gaps in housing codes, sanitation regulations, and enforcement policies. They should work with legal counsel and relevant officials to address these gaps and develop strategies to effectively use existing authorities to mitigate health hazards in homes. Evaluating program experience involves assessing agency resources, infrastructure, and personnel expertise. Programs should consider obtaining the Healthy Homes Specialist Credential and developing mechanisms to address social service needs, as these are often intertwined with housing issues. Partnerships are crucial for addressing community needs. Programs should identify issues they can address with existing resources and seek partnerships with organizations that can help tackle other concerns. Engaging faith-based and neighborhood organizations is particularly important for addressing disparities in low-income and underserved populations. Partnerships should be formalized through agreements that define roles and responsibilities. A referral process is integral to Healthy Homes programs. This includes identifying, addressing, and resolving housing issues, as well as documenting activities and outcomes. Follow-up care is essential for ensuring that identified hazards are remediated. Programs should monitor properties with unresolved issues and provide case management for conditions like lead poisoning or asthma. Surveillance systems should track housing variables and document interventions to assess their impact over time. Program evaluation is critical for continuous quality improvement. Evaluations should focus on process, outcomes, and impact to determine whether activities are implemented as planned and achieving their intended effects. Developing SMART objectives and using logic models can help design effective evaluation frameworks. The Healthy Homes strategic plan should address issues identified during the needs assessment and include goals, measurable objectives, and timelines. It should define roles and responsibilities, evaluate health impacts, communicate information effectively, and strengthen collaborations with other programs. Programs are encouraged to adopt evidence-based interventions and learn from previous research and successful initiatives. Developing a Healthy Homes program requires time, resources, and strong collaboration. The CDC’s HHLPPB remains committed to improving public health through the promotion of healthy homes.
